abstract: The author studies the characteristics of two leading candidates for the radio channel assignment method in personal communications services (PCS) systems: the quasi-static autonomous frequency assignment (QSAFA) method and the dynamic channel allocation (DCA) method. The author first describes channel planning, the QSAFA method, and the DCA method. The author then discusses the characteristics of these two methods in terms of link setup and automatic link transfer, synchronization requirement, implementation complexity for multiple service providers, spectrum efficiency and signal quality, and other relevant issues.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: International standards on universal personal telecommunications: state of the art and future projections
publicationTitle: 1st International Conference on Universal Personal Communications - ICUPC '92 Proceedings
abstract: World-wide standards on UPT (universal personal telecommunications) are of paramount importance: fortunately UPT implementations are not yet in place, so that instead of traditional standardization, whose purpose is to strengthen existing practice or to effect variety reduction on existing products, for UPT there is prospective standardization, which anticipates the products appearance in reality. However, UPT embryos are around the corner, like the SIM (subscriber identity module) in GSM or such services as advanced freephone, advanced call forwarding, automatic credit card calling. Therefore, a good timing is critical for the forthcoming UPT standards. The authors analyze the situation in international standardization bodies starting from ETSI, where work on UPT is proceeding at a fast pace (a standardization for Phase 1 has been approved), continuing with CCITT, where UPT activities are somewhat hindered by their being spread across a number of separate groups, even though some of the members are extremely active in the field, finally looking at the USA situation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Activities of the Cellular Telecommunications Industry Association microcell/microsystems subcommittee regarding microcell technology
publicationTitle: 1st International Conference on Universal Personal Communications - ICUPC '92 Proceedings
abstract: Discusses the activities of the Cellular Telecommunications Industry Association (CTIA) Microcell/Microsystems Subcommittee regarding microcell technology. The subcommittee was chartered to develop documents which would define the cellular carriers' viewpoints regarding microcells/microsystems and their applications to the equipment vendors. A brief history of the subcommittee is given, followed by summaries of the 'Microcell Guidelines' document and the 'Microcell/Microsystems Users' Performance Requirement'.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Service mobility/transparency for personal communications
publicationTitle: 1st International Conference on Universal Personal Communications - ICUPC '92 Proceedings
abstract: Personal communications services require that subscriber services be made available to users independent of their physical location. Services can be separated into their components of feature construct, common data, and user-specific data. Mobility can also be separated into local roaming, within the network provider's common control area, across control areas, and across providers. The author discusses the pros and cons of several approaches to providing service mobility/transparency: using an advanced intelligent network (AIN) to bring service profile data to the mobile user; using an intelligent loop distribution arrangement to bring the user's connection always back to their 'home' service logic area; and using an AIN to provide a limited, but ubiquitous, set of call processing features to users.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On the concept of a service host for personal communications services
publicationTitle: 1st International Conference on Universal Personal Communications - ICUPC '92 Proceedings
abstract: Personal communications services will be provided by new network capabilities. In addition to the substantial signaling network and related systems to provide personal communications services, there will be a need for services based on provision of a voice or data connection to a service-providing element, or service host. The author describes some possible functions of a service host and gives a description of one of several possible advanced intelligent network configurations to meet this need.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Advanced intelligent network requirements for personal communications services
publicationTitle: 1st International Conference on Universal Personal Communications - ICUPC '92 Proceedings
abstract: The advanced intelligent network (AIN) will be required to support a new service infrastructure called personal communications services (PCS). The authors describe the features of AIN which can be used to support PCS. They also identify the additional service capabilities needed in AIN and the SS7 network to support wide area PCS.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An efficient TDMA radio link and architecture for wireless local access
publicationTitle: 1st International Conference on Universal Personal Communications - ICUPC '92 Proceedings
abstract: A wireless digital loop architecture suitable for both portable and fixed subscribers is proposed using a low-delay 2 millisecond TDMA frame structure. This allows the elimination of echo cancelling circuits for voice applications when connecting to 2-wire transmission facilities. Each fixed radio transceiver supports up to 10 voice circuits using 32 kbps ADPCM speech coding. The resulting low-delay and high quality speech is appropriate for low-power wireless local access. For the fixed equipment, all per user baseband functions are located at central facilities to permit 'shoe-box' size radio ports or base stations. An important flexibility permitted by this TDMA architecture is low-complexity radio ports spread over a large serving area which can be connected to centralized facilities over low rate digital lines such as T-1 spans. Experimental circuits demonstrating these proposals are described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: CDMA versus dynamic TDMA for access control in an integrated voice/data PCN
publicationTitle: 1st International Conference on Universal Personal Communications - ICUPC '92 Proceedings
abstract: The authors present a comparative evaluation of dynamic TDMA and spread spectrum CDMA approaches to medium access control (MAC) in an integrated voice/data PCN environment. After a brief discussion of general technological issues related to the selection of a MAC approach for PCN, dynamic TDMA and packet CDMA protocols appropriate for the support of integrated voice/data traffic are described. Performance evaluation methodologies for determining the system capacities of these competing MAC techniques are described. System-level performance measures such as channel utilization, voice blocking probability and data delay are obtained from a detailed simulation model for the D-TDMA case, and compared with a preliminary set of corresponding results for asynchronous packet CDMA. Overall, the results show that while CDMA does achieve a higher normalized capacity than TDMA, the gains are very sensitive to the propagation loss constant, and must be balanced against higher message transfer delay for certain data services.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
